strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and under-explored problem: ReID features inherited from person re-identification are optimized for a different objective (distinguishing all identities globally) than what MOT association needs (separating similar identities within one sequence). The motivation is well argued and supported by clear feature-space visualizations (Fig. 1, Fig. 3).

The proposed solution is simple, training-free, and principled: applying Fisher Linear Discriminant with historical trajectory features as class conditions, plus a temporal-shifted centroid and a knowledge-integration term that balances the specialized and original spaces. Each component is well motivated and analyzed.

Experimental evidence is broad and convincing: consistent improvements on DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, and TAO, plus zero-shot transfer with MASA models across four model variants, demonstrating the method generalizes across feature extractors and is not tied to a particular tracker.

The ablation studies are thorough and insightful: the FLD vs. PCA comparison (Tab. 5) directly validates that the gain comes from discriminative, class-aware projection rather than dimensionality reduction; history length T, temporal shift coefficient λ0, and fusion coefficient α are all carefully examined.

The use of a deliberately naive ReID-only baseline (single-stage, EMA update, Hungarian matching) isolates the contribution of the proposed transformation from tracker engineering; the ablation hyperparameters are fixed across datasets, strengthening the fairness of the claims.

Good reproducibility posture: implementation details, hyperparameters, inference speed analysis (including the eigendecomposition bottleneck and potential GPU speedups), and an honest limitations section are provided; code release is promised.
weaknesses: The core technique (Fisher Linear Discriminant / LDA) is a classical, well-understood method. The novelty lies in its adaptation and the empirical insight rather than a new algorithm; some reviewers may view the technical depth as limited, though the application insight and systematization (temporal shift, knowledge integration) add legitimate value.

Comparison fairness concerns: the †-marked results indicate dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning for the proposed tracker, while baseline numbers are taken from their original papers (with potentially different detections). Although the gains over the authors' own untuned baseline are large and clearly reported, head-to-head SOTA comparisons should ideally control for detection inputs and tuning budgets.

The MOT17 gains are modest (e.g., 63.5 HOTA vs. 64.5+ for DiffMOT and MixSort variants), and the method's benefit is mainly concentrated on appearance-similar scenarios (DanceTrack, SportsMOT). The paper acknowledges this, but the practical impact on conventional crowded pedestrian tracking is less clear.

Scalability and robustness concerns of FLD in the online setting are not fully analyzed: the number of effective classes (active trajectories) and rank constraint (D' ≤ C−1) vary over time; behavior with very few trajectories, highly fragmented/ID-switching trajectories (where historical features may be mislabeled due to association errors), or long occlusions is only implicitly addressed. A failure-mode analysis of when contaminated history hurts the projection would strengthen the work.

The eigendecomposition is performed on CPU via scipy, which limits efficiency (22.7 FPS); the authors report a pending CuPy feature request rather than a resolved engineering solution, so real-time deployment claims are qualified.

Some design choices appear empirical (T=60, λ0=0.9, α=0.9 chosen by grid search per dataset) without theoretical justification; a sensitivity/transfer analysis of these hyperparameters across datasets would help demonstrate the defaults are robust rather than tuned.

strengths: The core observation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: generic ReID representation spaces are suboptimal for MOT because within-sequence targets occupy a small, hard-to-separate region of the space. Figures 1 and 3 provide intuitive visual support for this claim.

The proposed solution is simple, training-free, and plug-in: applying a Fisher Linear Discriminant projection using historical trajectory features as conditions, plus a temporally-weighted centroid and a weighted fusion of original/transformed similarities. This makes the method easy to adopt and reproducible.

Experimental coverage is broad and mostly convincing: DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, and zero-shot transfer to TAO with MASA features. The PCA-vs-FLD ablation (Table 5) directly supports the design choice that class-discriminative projection (not just dimensionality reduction) is what matters, and ablations on T, lambda_0, and alpha are thorough.

The paper is honest about its design philosophy: it deliberately uses a naive single-stage ReID-only tracker to isolate the effect of the proposed transformation, and it discusses limitations (no position cue, CPU eigendecomposition cost) explicitly.
Zero-shot results (Table 4) show consistent gains across four detector/segmenter variants, which strengthens the generality claim beyond a single tuned setup.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially classical Fisher Linear Discriminant (1936) applied per-sequence to trajectory features, plus an exponential decay weight and a scalar-blended similarity. Each component is standard; the contribution is primarily an application insight rather than a new algorithmic idea, which limits its significance for a top-tier venue unless the empirical case is airtight.

Fairness of the state-of-the-art comparison is questionable. The dagger-marked results indicate per-dataset hyperparameter tuning, and the baseline tracker is intentionally naive (single-stage, ReID-only, Hungarian matching). While this isolates the module, claims of 'comparable to or better than state-of-the-art' (e.g., HAT-FastReID-MOT 61.2 HOTA on DanceTrack vs. DiffMOT 62.3, or 63.5 on MOT17 vs. DiffMOT 64.4) only hold after dataset-specific tuning against methods with substantially more machinery, weakening the headline claims.

Potential methodological fragility is not adequately analyzed. FLD's between-class scatter has rank at most C-1, so early in a sequence (very few trajectories, few historical samples per trajectory) the generalized eigenproblem is ill-conditioned. The paper reports inference speed but not how performance evolves with the number of active trajectories, nor failure behavior under ID switches that contaminate the 'classes' with wrong-history features — a risk the authors themselves acknowledge but do not quantify.

The temporal-shifted centroid (Eq. 9) is a fixed exponential decay applied uniformly; there is no adaptive mechanism for occlusion or appearance drift, and the ablation shows the gains over lambda_0 = 1.0 are modest (~1 HOTA). Similarly, the knowledge integration is a single scalar-weighted average, which reads as engineering rather than a principled fusion.

On MOT17 the authors themselves concede that motion estimation suffices and appearance adds little; the reported gains there are small and partly attributed to the gray-tuned rows, so the method's value is largely confined to appearance-similar benchmarks (DanceTrack/SportsMOT). The paper could state this scope more restrictively.

The reported improvements conflate several simultaneous changes in some comparisons (e.g., simplifying MASA's bi-softmax to cosine+Hungarian 'resulted in a slight improvement', adjusting alpha to 0.5 for MASA), making it harder to attribute gains purely to the proposed transformation.

The claimed contribution of 'encouraging reconsideration of ReID features in MOT' is a conceptual framing, but the evidence that this specific transformation is the right answer is thin given the above; a learned, lightweight adaptation baseline (e.g., a small online metric head) is absent, so the necessity of the training-free FLD formulation over learned alternatives is not established.

strengths: The core observation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: ReID features trained for general re-identification occupy a suboptimal subspace for distinguishing highly similar targets within a single sequence, and the visualizations in Figs. 1 and 3 convincingly support this claim.

The method is simple, elegant, and training-free: applying a classical Fisher Linear Discriminant to historical trajectory features requires no additional model training and fits naturally into the online tracking loop, making it broadly applicable to feature-based trackers.

Experimental evidence is broad and convincing: consistent improvements across DanceTrack, MOT17, SportsMOT, and TAO; state-of-the-art or competitive results among feature-based trackers; strong zero-shot transfer with MASA features; and the comparison against PCA (Tab. 5) isolates the contribution of the discriminant objective rather than dimensionality reduction per se.

Thorough ablations (history length T, temporal-shift coefficient lambda_0, integration coefficient alpha) with sensible defaults chosen once and reused across datasets, plus honest discussion of trade-offs (e.g., overly long history queues degrading results, overly small lambda_0 harming robustness).

The paper is well written and clearly positioned; the limitations section is meaningful rather than perfunctory, and the broader message (specializing appearance features for MOT rather than blindly reusing general ReID practice) is a valuable conceptual contribution to the field. Code release is promised, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited from an algorithmic standpoint: FLD is a classical technique, and the contributions are domain-specific adaptations (trajectory-as-class, temporal-shifted centroid, weighted fusion). The paper is best viewed as an Applied/Systems contribution; under that lens the empirical evidence is the primary justification, which it largely satisfies.

Potential error accumulation is not analyzed: the projection matrix is computed from historical features of trajectories that may contain ID switches or mismatched detections. The paper acknowledges this risk qualitatively (Sec. 3.4) but provides no quantitative analysis of how association errors contaminate FLD and how the system behaves under such corruption.

Some reported gains rely on per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (results marked with dagger), which weakens strict comparability with prior state-of-the-art numbers that may not have received equivalent tuning; the grid-searched baseline tracker is also intentionally simplistic, so it remains unclear how much of the benefit transfers to stronger hybrid trackers without re-engineering.

Practical overhead deserves more attention: the eigendecomposition cost, dependence on a CPU-based solver, and 22.7 FPS are discussed, but the analysis of a candidate GPU implementation is left speculative; also, the method needs a minimum number of trajectories/samples per sequence to be meaningful, and behavior at sequence start or with very few active targets is not characterized.
Societal impact is not discussed, which is common for tracking papers but could be briefly addressed given surveillance-adjacent applications.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight: the paper identifies a genuine conceptual gap—MOT requires discriminating a finite, closed set of identities within a sequence, whereas off-the-shelf ReID features are optimized for open-set universality—and supports this with a quantitative correlation analysis (δ_1000 vs. AssA) on two benchmarks (Fig. 2, Fig. 6).

The proposed solution is elegant, training-free, and conceptually simple: applying Fisher Linear Discriminant online with historical tracklets as pseudo-class labels, plus two sensible task-specific refinements (temporally-weighted centroids and knowledge integration with the original space).

Extensive and convincing experimental evidence: consistent gains across pure-ReID trackers (large HOTA/AssA improvements on DanceTrack and SportsMOT, SOTA on SportsMOT), plug-in gains on multiple hybrid trackers, multiple backbones via MASA, and additional datasets (MOT17, MOT20, TAO), demonstrating generality rather than dataset-specific tuning.

Thoughtful ablations: comparison against PCA and against an oracle supervised FLD (Tab. 5, Tab. 9) directly tests the core hypothesis that history-derived supervision—not just any projection—is the key factor; hyperparameter sensitivity is analyzed (Tab. 6-8, Appendix D).

Unusually honest and complete discussion of limitations, including modest gains on MOT17/TAO and in hybrid trackers, error propagation from noisy tracklet supervision, inference speed overhead (22.7 vs 46.5 FPS) with a concrete diagnosis, and unsuccessful technical attempts—this raises confidence in the reported results.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core method is classical LDA applied online with tracklet pseudo-labels; the two refinements (temporal weighting of centroids, score-level fusion with the original space) are incremental. The value rests primarily on the insight and empirical validation rather than algorithmic depth.

Reliance on self-reinforcing supervision: the projection matrix is fit from historical assignments produced by the same tracker, creating a potential positive-feedback loop where early association errors bias subsequent matching. The paper argues the statistical signal remains reliable and includes a supervised-FLD comparison, but a deeper analysis of error accumulation over long sequences or drift under heavy occlusion is not provided.

Practical scalability concerns: the projected dimension d' = N_traj - 1 and the per-frame eigendecomposition scale with the number of active trajectories; FPS drops roughly by half, and the paper defers GPU implementation of the generalized eigenproblem to future work. Behavior in very crowded scenes with many trajectories is only partially covered (MOT20 val).

Baseline comparability: gains are largest relative to the authors' own fortified FastReID-MOT baseline with per-dataset hyperparameter tuning († settings); some SOTA claims rest on a training-free plug-in to somewhat older trackers, and comparison with more recent trackers is explicitly limited (Appendix D).

Reproducibility would depend on released code; the method has several hyperparameters (T, λ0, α, plus tracker thresholds) whose default values are transferred across datasets, which is reassuring but a code release is important to verify.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: MOT association operates over a closed, per-video identity set, so globally-trained ReID features are suboptimal, and tracking history can serve as free supervision to adapt the feature space. The correlation analysis between δ_1000 discriminability and AssA (Fig. 2, Fig. 6) provides genuine empirical support for the motivation rather than relying on intuition alone.

Technically sound and transparent method description: the FLD-based transformation, temporally-weighted centroid, and similarity-level knowledge integration (Eq. 8) are all fully specified, and the 'training-free' nature makes the approach easy to understand and reproduce in principle.

Extensive and honest experimental evidence: results span DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, MOT20, multiple ReID backbones via MASA, and integration into several hybrid trackers. The ablations (Tab. 5–9) are carefully staged, include an oracle setting, and the 'supervised vs. history-aware' comparison (Tab. 9) is a thoughtful control that isolates the contribution of historical supervision over FLD itself.

Notable gains: +8.7 HOTA over a grid-search-tuned FastReID-MOT baseline on DanceTrack and a new ReID-only SOTA on SportsMOT, with consistent (if smaller) improvements on TAO, MOT17 and when plugged into hybrid trackers.

Above-average limitations discussion: the authors candidly report modest MOT17 gains, reduced improvements in hybrid trackers, slower inference (22.7 vs 46.5 FPS), and unsuccessful technical attempts in the appendix, which increases trust in the reported results.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core mechanism is classical Fisher Linear Discriminant applied per-video with tracklet pseudo-labels, plus exponential temporal weighting and a scalar similarity fusion. Each component is standard; the contribution is primarily an observation and a plug-in application rather than a new algorithmic idea, which may be seen as thin for a top-tier venue.

Self-constructed baseline: the main comparisons use a custom FastReID-MOT tracker built by the authors because 'no public ReID-only trackers are available'. While the grid-searched baseline strengthens the claim, headline SOTA statements (e.g., 'state-of-the-art' on SportsMOT) rest partly on comparisons against trackers not designed for that setting and, per Appendix D, against trackers from ~2 years ago.

The motivating correlation analysis has a circularity risk: δ_1000 uses ground-truth positive/negative trajectory assignments, so its link to AssA may partly reflect annotation rather than the feature space quality a real online tracker could exploit; the causal direction is asserted more than established.

Diminishing returns where it matters most: gains shrink to +2.0 HOTA on MOT17 and are described as limited for hybrid trackers (attributed to IoU-dominant assignment). The claim that the full potential of ReID is 'underestimated' is therefore only demonstrated under specific conditions (appearance-similar targets, appearance-only association).

Several justifications lean on claims that would benefit from more rigor: e.g., error-propagation through noisy historical tracklets is argued qualitatively ('the overall statistical signal remains reliable') without analysis of how ID-switch frequency degrades the FLD projection; no variance/multiple-run reporting is provided for the tracking results.

Inference speed roughly halves (46.5→22.7 FPS) due to CPU eigendecomposition; the authors defer GPU acceleration to future work, which weakens practical deployability claims for crowded scenes (per-trajectory computation cost is acknowledged but not quantified).
No explicit code release statement is given, which limits reproducibility of the carefully tuned baseline configuration that the results depend on.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: MOT only requires discriminating a closed set of identities within a single video, so generic open-set ReID features can be adapted to the specific sequence. The paper convincingly frames this as a per-sequence feature-space specialization problem.

The proposed solution is elegant and training-free: applying Fisher Linear Discriminant with historical tracklets as dynamic supervision is simple, principled, and novel in this context. The authors are upfront that the value lies in the framing and analysis, not in a complex new architecture.

The correlation analysis between feature discriminability (delta_1000) and AssA (Fig. 2, Fig. 6) provides direct empirical support for the central hypothesis, going beyond just showing end-task gains.

Very thorough experimental validation: DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, MOT20, TAO, plus integration into multiple hybrid trackers and the MASA framework across several visual backbones. Consistent gains across scenarios, with a new SOTA on SportsMOT using appearance-only tracking.

Strong ablations: FLD vs. PCA (Tab. 5), supervised vs. history-aware FLD (Tab. 9, an especially convincing experiment showing cross-video labels do not transfer), history length T, temporal decay lambda_0, and fusion coefficient alpha.

Honest and extensive limitations discussion (Appendix C, D): reduced gains on MOT17/TAO where features are already discriminative, halved inference speed (22.7 vs 46.5 FPS), inability to apply to end-to-end trackers, and unsuccessful technical attempts. This transparency strengthens credibility.

The baseline appears carefully constructed (grid-searched hyperparameters for the baseline, fixed settings for ablations), and results without fine-tuning markers are transferred across datasets, supporting generalization of the hyperparameter choices.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter protocol raises some fairness concerns: baseline hyperparameters are grid-searched per dataset to maximize performance, and some SOTA comparisons involve dataset-specific fine-tuning (dagger/asterisk markers). While the authors argue this isolates their contribution, the exact tuning policy relative to prior work is not fully comparable and could inflate the apparent baseline strength or the reported deltas.

Potential feedback-loop risk is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed: the FLD projection is supervised by noisy historical tracklets, and erroneous assignments could bias subsequent projections. The paper asserts the 'overall statistical signal remains reliable' but provides no analysis (e.g., degradation under injected ID-switch noise or error-propagation curves over sequence length).

Method simplicity cuts both ways: FLD, temporally-weighted centroids, and score-level fusion are all standard techniques. The contribution is primarily a conceptual re-framing plus careful engineering; reviewers valuing algorithmic novelty may find the technical depth limited, although the paper's declared framing (Concept & Feasibility plus practical method) makes this acceptable.

Inference speed drops roughly by half (46.5 to 22.7 FPS) due to CPU eigenvalue computation; the mitigation discussion (GPU eigensolvers, dimensionality reduction) is deferred as engineering, and no optimized numbers are reported.

Gains are strongly conditioned on the regime of low initial feature discriminability (DanceTrack, SportsMOT); on MOT17 improvements are modest (+2.0 HOTA) and on TAO marginal. The method's practical value is thus somewhat dataset-specific, though the authors explain and visualize why.

Some clarifications would help reproducibility: details of the per-frame FLD re-fitting schedule, numerical regularization of scatter matrices when few frames per tracklet are available early in a sequence, and the statistical significance of the delta_1000-AssA correlation are only partially described in the main text.
